extracted.intended_audience: students, poets/dramatists, and literary critics studying poetic and dramatic composition (classical poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging poetry/drama (especially tragedy and epic): diction, metaphor, word-formation, unity and plot structure, metre, length, and the effects language should produce. Draws on Aristotle's Poetics with examples and anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (effects produced by language)
rubrics_metrics.description: All that concerns 'Thought' — the effects to be produced by the language: proof and refutation, the arousing of feelings like pity, fear, anger, exaggeration and depreciation; these effects apply equally to incidents and speeches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some effects must be clear without explanation, whereas others are produced in the speeches by the speaker and are due to the speeches. The rules for producing pity, terror, exaggeration, probability, etc., that apply to speeches also apply when arranging incidents. See Rhetoric for detailed treatment of 'thought.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: modes of speech (elocutional forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Diction know the various modes of speech: what is a command, a prayer, a statement, a threat, a question, an answer, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This knowledge properly belongs to elocution or an orator's craft; ignorance of such modes brings little serious censure on a poet, but the poet should be aware how different speech-modes function to achieve effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: basic linguistic components and phonetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is made up of letter, syllable, conjunction, joint, noun, verb, case, phrase; letters differ (vowel, semivowel, mute), syllables and accent matter for metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The detailed study of letters, syllables, and related phonetic matters properly concerns students of metre; these components influence diction and metrical possibilities and so are relevant to poetic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit of diction: clarity balanced with distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The merit of diction is to be clear and not commonplace: the clearest diction uses ordinary words (but may be commonplace); unfamiliar words give dignity but may create riddles or jargon. A mixture is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary words give clarity; rare words, metaphors, lengthening, and ornament give dignity. If a poet uses only unusual devices the result can be a riddle (if mostly metaphor) or jargon (if mostly rare words). Use a balanced mix to obtain both clarity and distinction. Examples: contrast an Aeschylus line with an Euripides variant to see effect; riddle example (‘I saw a man weld bronze upon a man with fire’ — answer: a cupping-bowl).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rare words, metaphors, and formal licences
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices that make diction 'unfamiliar' include rare words, metaphor, lengthening, ornament, invention, and alteration of words; these produce distinction if used moderately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lengthening, abbreviation, and alteration can aid clarity/distinction if part of the usual form is retained. Overuse (e.g., systematic lengthening or excessive rare words/metaphors) becomes ridiculous or comic; moderation is a requisite common to all kinds of writing. Parodic excesses (e.g., Eucleides) show the anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor: types and centrality to excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the application of a strange term (transferred from genus to species, species to genus, one species to another, or by analogy); metaphor by analogy operates when B is to A as D is to C and D is used instead of B. Metaphor is 'the token of genius.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor is the greatest single device for diction; the right use is largely unteachably tied to an eye for resemblances. Examples: calling a cup 'Dionysus's shield' or evening 'life's setting sun.' Metaphors can be formed even when the exact analogical term is absent. Metaphor is especially prized in some genres (see genre-specific suitability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invented, lengthened, curtailed, and altered words
rubrics_metrics.description: An invented word is coined by the poet and not used by others; 'lengthened' uses a longer syllable than usual; 'curtailed' shortens part of a word; 'altered' changes part of a word while leaving the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such coinages and modifications can create distinction and novelty, but should preserve part of the usual form to retain clarity. Examples cited: coined forms like 'sprouters' for horns; examples of lengthening/curtailing and altered forms. Again, moderation is advised; critics who mock such licence may be mistaken when the device is used well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate diction (nouns and devices suited to each genre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different poetic genres favor different kinds of nouns/devices: double forms suit dithyrambs; rare words suit heroic (epic) verse; metaphors suit iambics (and iambic verse, being imitation of speech, prefers ordinary words, metaphor, and ornament).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction to genre: heroic hexameter allows more rare words/forms; iambics (imitative of speech) require words plausible in speech. The same device may have differing effects in different metres/genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (single, whole, complete plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story must be constructed dramatically around a single piece of action, whole and complete in itself, with a beginning, middle, and end — like a single organism producing its peculiar pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid narratives that are simply historical collections of events or sequences in time that do not converge to a single result. Use one unified thread (as in parts of Homer) rather than many loosely related incidents. Tragedy and narrative must present one coherent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic constituent requirements (reversals, discoveries, calamities, thought and diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic must be simple or complex, or turn on 'character' or on 'calamity'; constituent parts are the same as tragedy except song and spectacle. Epic needs reversals and discoveries and calamities; thought and diction must also be good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose epic with the same structural concerns as tragedy (reversals, recognitions) but allow the narrative advantages (see variety and simultaneity). Homer exemplifies use of complex/simple forms and appropriate diction and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate length (comprehensibility and viewability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Length must allow the beginning and end to be embraced in one view; epic length should not exceed what prevents a reader/audience from grasping the unity — it may be longer than a single tragic performance but not so long as to lose unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical limits: works should be short enough to grasp their unity at once; ancient festivals presented three tragedies in sequence, implying constraints. Epic can increase bulk through relevant incidents, but beware exceeding what the audience can hold as a single work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metre (heroic hexameter for epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience shows the heroic hexameter is the right metre for epic; composing a narrative poem in any other metre or in several metres gives the wrong effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a consistent, genre-appropriate metre. Departures from the heroic hexameter in epic or mixing metres are judged improper for the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and relevance of incidents (avoid monotony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic may portray several parts of the story as occurring simultaneously and, if the incidents are relevant, they increase richness and variety; monotony quickly satiates an audience and causes failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include diverse but relevant incidents to enrich narrative and prevent monotony; do not insert unrelated episodes merely to enlarge bulk — incidents should contribute to the single action or to the poem's diversity in a meaningful way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in stylistic licence and avoidance of obtrusive excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtrusive use of licences (e.g., excessive lengthening of syllables, constant rare-word usage) is ridiculous; moderation is a requisite common to all kinds of writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include parodies that exaggerate a device to comedic effect (e.g., Eucleides' burlesque or later parodies). Use licences sparingly and purposefully; excessive use turns intended dignity into mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of speeches versus incidents to produce effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish effects produced by situation/incidents from those produced in speeches: some effects must be clear without explanation, while others are produced by the speeches of characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange where an emotional or argumentative effect should be realized — through the situation itself or through the characters' language. The orator's art (rhetoric) guides the production of effects in speech, complementary to dramatic arrangement.
